correctness.rationale: A minimum-degree first-force argument determines every candidate optimum: one of two endpoint-centered k-subsets on path powers, or a cyclic 2k-subset from a length-(2k+1) window containing its center. Each candidate has an explicit successful propagation sequence. Counting intersections of the exhaustive families determines path components and cycle configuration count; a complete center-separation edge classification yields n(k+1)(2k-1) cycle edges at n>=2k+4. A standalone Python checker independently enumerated all minimum-size candidates, ran sequential/simultaneous forcing, and reconstructed token-jump graphs for 35 path and 15 cycle cases, with further structural checks through k=7, n=45. These are corroboration rather than infinite proofs.

value.rationale: The established scalar minima alone do not explain whether optimum zero-forcing sets can be exchanged. A natural canonical infinite family has a sharp and permanent split into two components as path length grows, whereas the same operation on corresponding cycle powers remains connected, with n(2k-1) states, a chain of overlapping cliques, and exact n(k+1)(2k-1) exchanges. This is a motivated structural solution-space classification rather than a parameter renaming or arbitrary finite enumeration.
